bib.title: Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit: Disentangling Evolution Capabilities in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
bib.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit: Disentangling Evolution Capabilities in Self-Evolving LLM Agents", Minhua Lin, Juncheng Wu et al. (Penn State, UC Santa Cruz, Amazon and others), arXiv:2605.30621v1 [cs.AI], 28 May 2026. It reads as a preprint, and the extraction shows no venue.

COVERAGE: 82,835 of 82,835 chars read, covering main text, limitations, ethics, references (skimmed) and appendices B to E (tables 4 to 14). Appendices A.1 and A.2 (extended related work) were not seen; the main text points to them, and the extraction either omits them or I did not locate them. The Appendix B.1 dataset statistics table (Tab. 4) was also not seen. Text extraction is clean apart from the figures. Page numbers below are approximate.

I also read the target note. Its "Measuring the evolve loop itself" section cites this paper correctly in outline. Three places where it goes beyond the paper are listed under LIMITS.

CLAIMS (ranked)

1. Harness-updating is flat in base capability.
- number: spread between best and worst evolver is at most 3.1 pp on any benchmark.
- setup: 7 evolvers, 3 anchor agents (Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3-235B), 3 benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified 500 tasks, MCP-Atlas 500 tasks, SkillsBench 86 tasks). Skills-only edits on SWE and SB; skills, prompts and append-only memory on MCP. The evolver prompt and trajectory window are fixed. Pass rate, in-situ.
- quote: "The gap between the best and worst evolver is at most 3.1 percentage points (pp) on any benchmark, and no model wins across benchmarks."
- where: Sec 4.2, p5.

2. The smallest evolver matches the frontier evolver on SB.
- number: Qwen3.5-9B 3.8 pp vs Opus 4.6 2.3 pp vs Qwen3-235B 1.5 pp on SB.
- quote: "The smallest evolver, Qwen3.5-9B, posts the highest gain on SB (3.8 pp), exceeding both Opus 4.6 (2.3 pp) and Qwen3-235B (1.5 pp)."
- where: Sec 4.2, p5.
- Related: the ranking reshuffles by benchmark. Quote: "Qwen3-235B illustrates this reshuffling: it leads on SWE (8.2 pp) but ranks last on MCP (0.6 pp)."
- Case study (Fig 4, App C.2): on SkillsBench flink-query with an Opus 4.6 agent, the score was 0.67 with no skill and 1.0 with a skill from either Qwen3.5-9B or Opus 4.6. Quote: "the two skills ... are procedurally isomorphic". The two skills encode the same five steps. This is one task, a case study.

3. The agent, not the evolver, dominates post-evolution score.
- number: within-agent spread across 7 evolvers is at most 5.1 pp (MCP, Qwen3-235B) against a 36.0 pp base gap between Opus and Qwen3-235B. Across all three benchmarks, the strong agent paired with its worst evolver still beats the weak agent paired with its best evolver by 18.6 to 35.2 pp.
- quote: "The within-agent spread across seven evolvers is at most 5.1 pp (Qwen3-235B), small against the 36.0 pp gap between the Opus and Qwen3-235B base capabilities."
- quote: "the strong agent still leads by 18.6 to 35.2 pp on every benchmark."
- where: Sec 4.2, p5-6; Tab 6, App C.3.
- Other benchmarks: within-agent spread is 5.0 pp on SWE and 9.3 pp on SB. The between-agent gap exceeds the spread by 11x on SWE and only 2.2x on SB.

4. Harness-benefit is non-monotonic in base capability.
- number: SWE gain is 19.3 pp for Qwen3-235B (base 20.7%), 4.4 pp for Qwen3-32B (base 3.6%), 2.6 pp for Opus 4.6 (base 74.2%). On MCP the peak is GPT-OSS-120B at 7.0 pp (base 28.0%).
- setup: 6 task agents. Benefit = max gain over 3 anchor evolvers (Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3-235B). In-situ pass rate.
- quote: "On SWE, the gain peaks at Qwen3-235B (19.3 pp), while the weaker Qwen3-32B gains only 4.4 pp and the stronger Opus 4.6 gains only 2.6 pp."
- where: Sec 4.3 Obs 1, p6, Tab 1.
- Other SWE gains from Tab 7: GPT-OSS-120B 15.8, Haiku 4.5 2.4, Sonnet 4.6 2.8.
- Caveat the paper concedes: "SWE and MCP provide the clearest evidence for the non-monotonic harness-benefit pattern, while SB suggests that the low-base regime can be more variable across task domains." On SB, Haiku 4.5 gains the most (15.1 pp), Qwen3-235B only 1.1 pp, and Qwen3-32B 5.8 pp.

5. Activation failure: weak models do not load skills.
- number: skill-load rate (SLR) is 0.251 for Qwen3-32B and 0.446 for GPT-OSS-120B, against 0.957 to 0.961 for Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 and Qwen3-235B (Haiku 4.5 0.794).
- setup: SkillsBench only, fraction of trajectories that load at least one skill. The no-evolution baseline starts from an empty skill set.
- quote: "the skill-load rate is near ceiling for Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, and Qwen3-235B (0.957–0.961), but drops to 0.446 for GPT-OSS-120B and 0.251 for Qwen3-32B."
- where: Sec 4.3, p7, Tab 2.
- Mechanism (Fig 7, App D.1): Qwen3-32B bundled `analysis`, `plan` and `load_skill` into one multi-key JSON action, and the runner's single-key format gate rejected it, so the skill never entered context. This is a protocol or format failure, not a failure to identify the skill.

6. Adherence failure: loading is not sufficient.
- number: harness-following rate (HFR) is 0.757 for Opus 4.6 and 0.142 for Qwen3-32B. Qwen3-235B has SLR 0.961 but HFR 0.350. Pass-when-loaded (LPR) is 0.022 for Qwen3-235B and 0.177 for Opus 4.6.
- setup: SkillsBench. HFR is judged by Claude Sonnet 4.6 against a rubric extracted from the skill body. Trajectories are blinded.
- quote: "Qwen3-235B provides the cleanest separation between activation and adherence: its skill-load rate is 0.961, nearly identical to Opus 4.6, yet its HFR is only 0.350."
- where: Sec 4.3, p7, Tab 2.
- Full Tab 2 (SLR / HFR / LPR): Qwen3-32B 0.251/0.142/0.023; GPT-OSS-120B 0.446/0.442/0.040; Haiku 4.5 0.794/0.600/0.099; Qwen3-235B 0.961/0.350/0.022; Sonnet 4.6 0.959/0.730/0.145; Opus 4.6 0.957/0.757/0.177.
- Fig 7 adherence case: Qwen3-32B treated a fallback chain as a literal script and gave up at turn 10 with task_complete=true.

7. Adherence decays over a trajectory, and more steeply for weak models.
- number: Qwen3-32B goes 0.52 (harness loaded) to 0.22 (mid turn) to 0.13 (final turn), a drift of -0.39. GPT-OSS-120B goes 0.67 to 0.43 (-0.24). Opus 4.6 goes 0.89 to 0.80 (-0.09).
- setup: LLM-judge 0–1 phase adherence, Sonnet 4.6 as judge, SkillsBench.
- quote: "Qwen3-32B drops sharply from 0.52 after harness loading to 0.13 at final validation, while GPT-OSS-120B drops more moderately from 0.67 to 0.43. In contrast, Opus 4.6 remains stable, from 0.89 to 0.80."
- where: Sec 4.3, p8, Tab 3.
- The intro says adherence "decays across the trajectory over four times more steeply than strong models" (0.39 vs 0.09 is about 4.3x).

8. Design guidance from the authors.
- Spend capability budget on the task-solving agent, not the evolver.
- Train harness invocation into agents.
- Strengthen long-horizon instruction following.
- quote: "Allocate capability budget to the task-solving agent, not the evolver."
- where: Sec 4.2 take-away, p6.

9. Mid-tier models benefit most, strong models are near a ceiling.
- Explanation: ceiling effect at the top. At the bottom the paper argues it is not headroom but the activation and adherence failures.
- Caveat: the ceiling-effect explanation is the authors' reading, not tested.

LIMITS
- Authors concede:
  - Only harness evolution is studied. No fine-tuning, RL or hybrid methods.
  - The model grid is "representative but not exhaustive".
  - The Ethics statement warns that bad lessons can persist in the harness. Evolvers were barred from editing evaluation scripts or weights; tools/ is read-only.
- Evaluation is in-situ. The same task stream drives evolution and scoring. Each task is scored under H(t-1) before its evidence is used, so a task is never scored under a harness derived from itself. But this is an online-stream gain, not a held-out gain. The note's "Held-out task gain" metric is not what this paper measures.
- Statistical power:
  - No confidence intervals or seeds are reported in the extraction.
  - SB has 86 tasks (SkillsBench scores are averaged over 5 trials, but reported pp values land near multiples of 1.16), so single-task swings are large. The paper itself calls the SB trend "noisier in the low-base regime".
  - Base rates of 0.0% on SB (Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B) make gains hard to interpret.
- The mechanism analysis (SLR, HFR, phase drift) is SkillsBench only, with LLM-judged adherence (judge is Sonnet 4.6, a family member of the strong tier). Only three models were used for phase drift.
- The benefit metric is the maximum over 3 anchor evolvers, so it is biased upward and is not a mean.
- The updating metric uses only 3 anchor agents.
- Model names are the 2026 versions (Opus 4.6, Qwen3.5-9B) and will date.
- Where the note goes beyond the paper:
  - The note's "two-way model swap" recipe with three conclusions ("every model regresses -> suspect the change") is the note's own construction. The paper does fix the evolver and vary the agent, and fix the agent and vary the evolver, but gives no such diagnostic table.
  - The note's four metrics (candidate-change validity, activation rate, adherence rate, held-out gain) are not the paper's metrics. The paper defines harness-updating, harness-benefit, SLR, HFR and LPR. "Candidate-change validity" does not appear in the extraction.
  - "Harness-updating is flat" is measured by downstream gain with a fixed agent, not by independent validation of the edit.

- Agrawal et al., 2026 (GEPA).

CODE: none. Judge prompt templates are in Tabs 10 to 14: evolver system prompt Tab 10, HFR rubric extraction Tab 12, trajectory judging Tab 13, phase-adherence prompt Tab 14 (5 phases: skill_loaded, first_action, midpoint, pre_final, final_validation). The Tab 10 evolver instruction "Prefer concise, reusable updates over task-specific patches" may be worth citing, but the paper reports no ablation of it.

FIGURES (not extracted via the figures script; captions taken from the text)
- Fig 2, p2: overview. (A) updating is flat, (B) benefit is non-monotonic, weak models fail at activation and adherence. A good one-glance summary.
- Fig 3, p5: bar charts of Δupdate per evolver on SWE, MCP and SB. Shows the flat spread and the reshuffled best and worst evolver.
- Fig 4, p6: flink-query, with no skill 0.67, Qwen3.5-9B skill 1.0, Opus skill 1.0. Shows the "isomorphic skills" claim concretely.
- Fig 5, p6 (and Fig 8, p15): dots for 7 evolvers per agent against the no-evolve tick. Shows that evolver variation is small next to agent variation.
- Fig 6, p7: Δbenefit versus base pass rate on SWE, a hump shape. The strongest single visual for non-monotonicity. MCP and SB analogues are Fig 9.
- Fig 7, p8: the two failure modes with turn-level traces (multi-key format gate; literal-script misread). The best candidate for the note.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Figure text is interleaved in the extraction (Fig 4 and Fig 7 are garbled), but the tables are readable.
- Appendix A and Tab 4 were not seen.
- I did not run the figures script, so the page numbers are approximate.
